outcomes: Names the pawn skeleton of the Closed Ruy Lopez and the holes each side has
Says what the lever d4 needs (c3, so that a pawn can recapture; h3 is a common preparation, not a requirement) and why Black should usually keep the tension rather than capture at once
Counts attackers and defenders of d4 after ...c5 and decides whether a capture gains anything
Names Black's three levers and the kind of position in which each is playable
Explains the structure to a beginner with the idea, when it works, an example and a warning

steps.caption: Closed Ruy Lopez, White to move. Both kings are castled. Look for open files, for pawns that touch each other, and for pawn moves each side could make. Nothing is explained yet.

claims.statement: No file is open or half-open: every file still holds a pawn.
Black's pawns on b5, d6 and e5 are each guarded by another pawn.

steps.prompt: Before reading on: name one pawn move you expect White to want here and one for Black, and what you think each costs.

steps.text: **Closed does not mean quiet.** In this position no file is open, because every file still holds a pawn. [I] So play happens in two places: behind the pawns, where pieces regroup, and at the pawn levers. A lever is a pawn move that attacks an enemy pawn and can change the structure. This lesson lists the levers, what each one costs, and when a side should take or keep the tension.

**Holes.** A hole is a square that none of your pawns can guard any more. [V] Black has two here, a5 and c6; White has one, d3. A hole is only a weakness if an enemy piece can settle there. [I] So ask who can reach the hole, not only whether you have one. Black's knight on c6 stands on one of its own holes, which is safe while it stays there.

**The lever d4.** The pawn on d4 attacks e5, so e5 now has two attackers. The pawn on c3 is what makes the lever work: it guards d4, so a black capture would be met by a recapture with a pawn. [I] The price is that e4 and d4 become targets, and Black's pieces can go after them. Watch what Black does with the knight that stood on c6.

steps.text: **What the capture gave away.** [I] exd4 cxd4 is an even pawn trade, but it gives White a free pawn pair on e4 and d4 while Black's pieces have no target. [H] A capture on d4 becomes better for Black when a piece can hit d4 or e4 at once, because then White's recapture costs something. Test the hypothesis before you capture: count the attackers of d4 and the defenders, then ask who recaptures.

steps.text: **Why not capture on c5?** [V] At depth 16 the engine rates dxc5 at least 70 centipawns below the best move. [I] dxc5 Nxc5 is an even pawn trade, but the knight recaptures with a tempo on the bishop on b3, and White's d4 pawn, which held the centre, is gone. A capture is a decision about who gets the tempo; the side that recaptures with a gain wins that decision.

steps.title: Keep or release the tension?
steps.prompt: Predict first: in the first position Black has several moves that keep d4 under pressure. In the second Black captures. Which side gains by the capture?

steps.text: **Closing with d5.** If White does not want to keep the tension, the pawn can advance. [I] The centre closes, and Black's reply ...c4 hits the bishop on b3 and gains space on the queenside. Neither side is forced: at depth 16 d5 is within 40 centipawns of Bc2, so the choice is a matter of plan, not of safety.

steps.text: **Black's three levers.** [I] ...c5 attacks d4; it is playable when a piece such as the knight on d7 can recapture on c5. ...exd4 changes the structure; it is playable when a piece can at once hit d4 or e4. ...d5 is a counter-centre; it needs e5 still defended by pieces. Played too early it costs about half a pawn on the engine's scale, and Black must find ...Nxe4 to win the pawn back. One structure shows the first lever through to its end.

steps.text: **What the open file means.** [I] Both sides can put a rook on the c-file, but only a rook with a safe square to enter benefits. Neither side has done so yet because the bishops on c1 and c8 are still at home. [H] The bishops tend to move first, and the side that finishes development with tempo, by attacking d4 or e4 as it moves, gets the file first. You can test that guess on the board below.

[V] The engine still has the position between level and about +0.8 for White at the end, so neither side clearly gained. A pawn move on the wing is a question, and a calm answer is often enough.

steps.text: **Levers and timing.** [I] A lever is a question to the other side: take, ignore or support. The side that plays it needs the supporting pieces behind it first; the side that answers must count before it captures. [H] In this opening the usual order is pieces first, lever second, capture last; the positions above fit that order, but they are a handful of examples, not a proof.

steps.text: **What the trade shows.** [V] After the rooks come off, the engine rates the position as roughly level. [I] A lever on the wing does not have to win material: it can trade pieces and pawns, open a file and reduce the risk to the side that is slightly worse. [H] For a learner, that makes the queenside lever a safe plan for either side when the centre is locked: you can aim for it without a tactic being required.

steps.text: **Self-check.** Did you say when a lever works (a pawn guards the square it lands on, and pieces stand ready), when it fails (the other side recaptures with a gain), give an example a beginner could set up, and name one mistake such as capturing on d4 or c5 too soon? The app grades nothing; compare your answer with these points.

**Recap.**
- Closed means every file still has a pawn; play is at the levers.
- A hole is a square your pawns cannot guard; ask who can reach it.
- White's levers: d4 (needs c3; h3 is a common preparation), later a4.
- Black's levers: ...c5, ...exd4 when prepared, ...d5.
- Count attackers and defenders, then ask who recaptures.
- Keep the tension until a capture gains something. [I]
